why: model -> drivers -> score the rest -> save the top 5
answers:
Here's what predicts churn in your data:

**The single biggest driver is support tickets** — they account for **~90%** of the predictive power. Each additional ticket strongly pushes a customer toward churning. Monthly usage (monthly_hours) is the second factor, but in the opposite direction: higher usage means lower churn risk. Plan type and tenure had almost no predictive impact.

The model (ridge regression) scored **AUC 0.88** — a strong predictor.

The **5 most at-risk active customers** have been saved to **at_risk.csv**:

| Customer | Tickets | Monthly Hours | Tenure | Plan | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C0007 | 5 | 21.0 | 29 mo | pro | **94.5%** |
| C0290 | 4 | 4.9 | 24 mo | basic | **89.7%** |
| C0312 | 4 | 17.1 | 31 mo | basic | **81.9%** |
| C0285 | 4 | 16.9 | 51 mo | basic | **72.2%** |
| C0107 | 3 | 5.2 | 48 mo | basic | **70.3%** |

C0007 and C0290 are the most urgent — both above 90%. C0007 is on a pro plan, so they may be especially valuable to retain.

**Caveats:** These are associations, not proven causes. The model was cross-validated on the same dataset, so the AUC might be slightly optimistic. The risk scores are estimates, not certainties — a quick review of each customer's recent support history could help validate.
